newsitem.title: NORWAY: Norway's Jagland says budget changes inevitable.
newsitem.headline: Norway's Jagland says budget changes inevitable.

text.p: Norway's new prime minister Thorbjoern Jagland said on Friday changes would have to be made to the 1997 state budget proposal for it to be accepted by a hostile parliament.
"We must realise that there will be changes to the budget, but we don't want to change the balance we have struck," he told a news conference after taking office.
"But clearly we can change some priorities, and it is possible to increase spending on some areas and still maintain the balance we have," he said.
The Labour minority government is under pressure from the opposition right and left of centre to increase expenditure before the budget is finally adopted in December.
"We want a state budget that is responsible and can mobilise a majority in parliament," Jagland said.
A majority in parliament wants to raise spending in the 1997 budget by about 7.0 billion crowns ($1.08 billion), partly through higher welfare payments and tax revisions.

Central bank governor Kjell Storvik said earlier this week any weakening of the 1997 state budget would be detrimental to a balanced economic development. He has urged parlament not to dilute the budget because there was a clear risk of further pressure on the economy and higher cost growth next year.

Oil-rich Norway's draft budget contains a 40.9 billion crown surplus. Despite the huge surplus projected for next year, the government has said it will keep a tight grip on the purse strings for fear of fuelling inflation.

Jagland reaffirmed his government would continue the economic policies of Prime Minister Gro Harlem Brundtland, who announced her resignation on Wednesday after a total of 10 years in office. ($1=6.460 Norwegian Crown)
"The pillar of the social welfare policy of this government is to keep on maintaining low price growth so that we can continue fighting unemployment," Jagland said.
The new premier, who has a history as a political left-winger, said it was up to politicians to limit market forces by using the steering controls they have through the state budget.

"The danger of pouring more oil money into the economy is that the market forces will take over, that inflation and interest rates unbalance the economy," Jagland said. "The market forces take over if the politicians give up control."
